newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa clothing stores race up on rate cut hopes.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa clothing stores race up on rate cut hopes.

text.p: Shares in South African clothing retailers raced ahead on Thursday, riding high on hopes of a cut in the country's high interest rates and putting recent poor earnings performances behind them.

But industry analysts warned that business in the clothing sector, which has been hard hit by high rates squeezing consumers, remained tough and that a reduction would have to come soon for stores to enjoy a robust Christmas shopping spree.

"The trading conditions are still pretty tough and we don't anticipate them getting a great deal easier without a reduction in interest rates," said Donald Etheridge, managing director of Edgars Ltd, one of the country's largest clothing firms.

"The only explanation I can give (for the share price rises) is that people are moving back in anticipation of a more than one percent reduction in interest rates and that they fear that it may be difficult to get shares nearer the date," he told Reuters.

A recent Reuters poll showed economists think a one-percentage-point rate cut possible before the end of the third quarter and a certainty by the end of the year amid increasing signs that South Africa's economy is slowing sharply.
The country's prime lending rate is currently 20.25 percent.

The Johannesburg Stock Exchange's stores sector, which is heavily laden with clothing shares, on Thursday advanced over 1.4 percent to a new high of 10,713, bringing its gains since the start of June to over 20 percent.

Edgars has risen from around 102 rand in early June to 132 rand on Thursday -- its best level since August last year. This is despite it reporting in May a five percent slide in annual attributable earnings as slow consumer spending pressured margins.

Other clothing shares have shown similar big gains recently. Heavyweight Foschini Ltd, whose year earnings to end-March slid sharply, has risen 25 percent since mid-June to touch 16.20 rand on Thursday. Wooltru Ltd has soared nearly 30 percent to 28.20 since early June.
But analysts warned that the market may be getting a little ahead of itself and that clothing-store shares were becoming expensive.
"People are reckoning they should get in now and there is nothing wrong with that argument, but I don't think that one should be getting in at these prices," he said.

They said that even with a trim in rates, spending on clothes would remain pressured as high income consumers invested more money in education and security and lower-income earners seemed to be buying more appliances and electronic goods.
